events.text: {npc}, a young acolyte of Cold Pine Temple with a shaved head and ink on {his} fingers, finds you in the market and does not let go of your sleeve. "The stone bodhisattva weeps again," {he} says. "Red tears. The pilgrims call it a miracle. The abbot will not look at it. I think it is something else, and nobody will listen to me."

mem.note: was listened to when no one else would

effects.log: {npc} talks for an hour without stopping. By the end you are curious, and {he} is grateful.
"A lie," {npc} says at once, and then looks frightened of {his} own words.
You shake your sleeve free. {npc} looks at you the way the young look at the old who disappoint them.

events.text: {npc} brings you the news of the weeping statue, and you are already nodding before {he} finishes. You have never been to Cold Pine Temple in this life. Your soul has: it remembers the cold of the stone floor, and an answer it found there once, the shape of it if not the words.

effects.log: You tell {npc} you will help. Somewhere under your ribs an old certainty settles in.
You keep the feeling to yourself. {npc} only sees that you agreed far too quickly.

events.text: You and {npc} keep watch in the temple hall for a week of nights. On the fourth night it rains, and by the small hours the bodhisattva's cheeks are wet and red. You touch the tears. They are cold, and they taste of iron, and they are coming from inside the stone.

choices.text: Lay your palm on the stone

effects.log: The stone is wet from within, like a sponge. Whatever feeds it runs behind the altar.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep the vigil for both of you

effects.log: {npc} sits up with the statue until dawn and swears it sighed once. You do not laugh at {him}.

events.text: Behind the altar, under a panel nobody has opened in decades, a clay pipe runs into the living rock of the mountain. Water seeps from the joints, rust-red. {npc} holds the lamp with shaking hands. "Someone built this," {he} whispers. "Someone built a miracle."

choices.text: Follow the pipe with your fingers

effects.log: It runs down, not up. Whatever made the tears flow also hid something beneath the floor.

choices.text: Put the panel back exactly as it was

effects.log: Nobody must know you were here yet. {npc} helps, careful as a thief.

events.text: The sect's records of Cold Pine Temple are dull until one line: sixty years ago the temple asked your sect for masons, for "repairs to the bodhisattva's foundation", and paid them twice the going rate to keep quiet. {npc} reads it over your shoulder and goes pale.

effects.log: You copy it in your own hand. A sect remembers what a temple would rather forget.

choices.text: Ask the archivist who signed it

effects.log: The name is the old abbot's teacher. The archivist asks why you want to know, and you do not answer.

events.text: The old abbot of Cold Pine Temple pours tea for you and {npc} with hands that will not keep still. When you name the old abbot's teacher, the cup goes over. The old man sits in the spilled tea for a long while, then says: "My teacher buried what could not be burned. Do not dig it up. Please."

effects.log: You thank the old abbot for the tea. {npc} walks out beside you in silence, and does not look back.
The old abbot looks at you as if you were the first kind thing in years.

events.text: You and {npc} dig beneath the bodhisattva by lamplight while the iron water drips on your backs. Under a flagstone lies a lacquer box, and in it a confession sixty years old: the abbot's teacher killed a pilgrim in a quarrel, and led the spring through the stone so that no one would ever dig where the body lay. The bodhisattva wept for sixty years so a murderer could sleep.

choices.text: Give the confession to the old abbot

mem.note: saw you show mercy to the old abbot

effects.log: The old abbot reads it twice and burns nothing. The next spring the pilgrims find a grave beside the statue, and a name on it.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the pilgrims

effects.log: The miracle dies in an afternoon. {npc} stands beside you through all of it, and the province talks of nothing else.

events.text: When the box comes up out of the earth, {npc} looks at you strangely. "You knew where to dig," {he} says. "Before the stone was even lifted. How?" You do not know how. Some part of you has stood in this hole before, in another body, with the same iron water running down its neck.

effects.log: "A past life," you say. {npc} does not laugh. {He} only nods slowly, as if a great many things are now explained.
{npc} does not believe you, and is too polite to say so.

events.text: Your answer goes round the temple and the town before nightfall, and it is the wrong one. Pilgrims shout at the gate; a monk who did nothing is spat on in the street. {npc} finds you afterwards. "It was not that," {he} says quietly. "I know it was not."

effects.log: You go to the gate and say you were wrong, loudly, where the pilgrims can hear. It helps a little.

choices.text: Hold your tongue and think again

effects.log: You go over every clue again. Somewhere in them is the thing you missed.

events.text: You wake with a memory that is not yours: a red gate with a crack in its left post, a well with a split wooden lid, and a child calling a name you have never heard. It is still there at breakfast. By noon you have told {npc}, a travelling scribe who collects strange stories, and {npc} is writing it down.

mem.note: was given the whole strange tale

effects.log: {npc} draws the gate from your words. When you look at the drawing, your hands go cold.

choices.text: Ask {npc} if it happens to others

effects.log: "Sometimes," {npc} says. "Usually to people who are about to find something."

choices.text: Decide it was only a dream

effects.log: You laugh it off. The memory stays anyway, but you stop speaking of it.

events.text: Three days north, in a village you have never seen, the red gate stands with a crack in its left post. {npc} stops dead in the road beside you. Your feet walked here before your eyes found it: every turn of the way, every stone. Beyond the gate is the well, and its lid is split exactly where you remember.

effects.log: The wood is warm in the sun. For a heartbeat you are someone else, older, coming home.
{npc} asks the villagers about the gate. Nobody remembers who painted it red.

events.text: The well-keeper's grandmother is very old and very sure. "A traveller," the old woman says, "long before your time. Stayed one winter. When spring came the traveller was gone, and there was a child in this house who called after them at the gate every evening for a year. That name you have, that was it."

choices.text: Ask what became of the child

effects.log: "Grew up. Had children. Their grandchildren still live by the well," the old woman says.

choices.text: Sit with the old woman a while

effects.log: You hear about the winter, and the traveller who sang badly and mended roofs. {npc} writes it all down.

events.text: In a temple register two valleys away, {npc} finds the name, and beside it a date of death. You read it twice. The traveller died the year before you were born. The memory is yours. It is only from before. The last piece of this is not in this life: whoever could answer it has not been born yet, or has not yet found you.

effects.log: {npc} promises to keep it, and the copy, and the drawing of the gate. "For whoever comes asking," {npc} says.

choices.text: Burn a stick of incense for the traveller

effects.log: You burn it for yourself, in a way. The smoke goes straight up, which the old people call a good sign.

events.text: You are young, and you have never been north, and still your feet stop at a red gate with a crack in its left post. The memory of it is older than this body. At the well stands {npc}, who looks at you a long time and then says, "I have a record for you. An old scribe left it in our family, for whoever came asking about the gate."

effects.log: It is your old name, your old death, a drawing of this gate. Your soul carried the question here. Now it can be answered.
"My grandmother's teacher," {npc} says. "The scribe said you would come, and that you would look exactly as lost as you do."

events.text: You stand at the red gate with {npc} and say it aloud: the name the child called was your own, in the life before this one, and the child was that life's child. From the house behind the well a grey-haired woman comes out to see who is talking. The grandchild of that life's child. The face of someone you loved, two lives ago, looks at you without knowing you.

choices.text: Say nothing, and help draw water

effects.log: You help with the bucket and the split lid. That is all. It is enough, and more than enough.

choices.text: Tell the family who you were

effects.log: They do not believe you. Then the grandmother makes you sing, and you sing badly, and the old woman sits down hard.

events.text: "No," {npc} says, when you give your answer. "That is not it. I have watched your face at that gate. Whatever this is, it is not a ghost and not a poison. Think again." The villagers you questioned look at you sideways now, and doors close when you pass.

choices.text: Go back to the gate alone

effects.log: You stand there until dark. The memory stirs, and says nothing.
You go house to house. Most forgive you. The well-keeper does not.

events.text: {npc}, an investigator for the county who has seen too many bodies to be surprised by one, buys you a bowl of noodles and lays two funeral notices on the table. Same name, Elder Baek of the Pine Gate School. Twenty years apart. "A man may die twice in a story," {npc} says. "Not in my county."

effects.log: The calligraphy is different, the wording the same, word for word. Someone copied the first for the second.

choices.text: Ask why {npc} brings it to you

effects.log: "Because the Pine Gate School will not talk to the county," {npc} says. "It might talk to the murim."

choices.text: Say the dead can stay buried

effects.log: {npc} finishes the noodles in silence and takes the notices back.

events.text: {npc} lays the two funeral notices on the table, and something in you goes still. Your soul has read notices like these before, in another life, and found the trick in them. You do not remember the answer. You remember that there was one, and that it was simpler than anyone wanted.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to look for the simple answer

effects.log: {npc} raises an eyebrow, and writes it down anyway.
You only nod. {npc} notices that you are not surprised.

events.text: The county keeps its dead in good order. Both death records for Elder Baek are signed by one physician, Dr. Hwang of the West Gate, twenty years apart, in the same careful hand. {npc} lays them side by side. "The same doctor," {he} says. "For the same patient. Twice."

choices.text: Find out if Dr. Hwang still lives

effects.log: Dr. Hwang lives, retired, at the edge of the city, and drinks.
There is none. But in the margin of the first, a different ink: "scars not seen".

events.text: Dr. Hwang is very old and very fond of pear brandy, and after the third cup the old doctor stops pretending. "The first body had the Elder's face," the doctor says, "and none of the Elder's scars. Not one. I wrote what the school told me to write. They paid well. You understand." {npc} understands, and writes it all down.

choices.text: Thank the doctor and leave money

effects.log: The old doctor weeps a little, and keeps the money.
"The Elder," the doctor says, "in person, a week after the burial."

events.text: The Pine Gate School's disciples will not let a stranger past the gate, but they bow to a master of your standing, and you walk in. Inside, in the hall of ancestors, Elder Baek's tablet has been carved twice: an old tablet, split, and a new one. {npc} stares at you. "I could not have done that in ten years," {he} says.

effects.log: On the back of the old one, a single carved character: "brother".
You bow to both. The disciples watching from the door relax a little.

events.text: The Pine Gate School's oldest ledger smells of mould and pine resin. In the founder's own hand: two sons born to the first Baek on the same night, in a year of famine. One was named. The other has only a line beside that birth, and the word "kept". {npc} reads it three times. "Kept where?" {he} asks. You think you know.

effects.log: Some families keep their shame in ledgers. This one kept a person.
{npc} folds the copy into {his} sleeve like a blade.

events.text: You lay it out for {npc}: the unnamed twin, raised in secret, died twenty years ago wearing the Elder's face, so the Elder could slip a blood debt and live on under the same name in the same school. The school buried a stranger first and the Elder second. At the Pine Gate, the disciples hear it and do not argue. They only take down the second tablet, and carve the first one anew, with two names.

choices.text: Ask that the twin be named

mem.note: saw you give a nameless man a name

effects.log: The school gives the twin a name at last, sixty years late. {npc} writes it into the county's books.

choices.text: Let the county have the glory

effects.log: {npc} takes the case to the magistrate and names you in the report. Your name goes round the county offices.

events.text: When you lay the answer out, {npc} sits back and looks at you for a long time. "You walked into a school that sees every outsider as an enemy," {he} says, "and they opened their ledger for you. They fear you, I think." Perhaps. The truth came out either way, and the Elder's old blood debt with it.

choices.text: Settle the old blood debt yourself

effects.log: You find the family the Elder wronged and pay them what you can. It does not buy anything back. It helps.
They are all dead now, wronged and wrongdoer. You leave the ledger closed.

events.text: The Pine Gate School answers your accusation with a formal letter, and the county with a reprimand to {npc}. "You were wrong," {npc} says, holding the reprimand, "and I put my name to it." {He} is not angry. {He} is tired, which is worse.

effects.log: You write to the magistrate yourself. The reprimand is withdrawn. {npc} notices.
Two funerals. One doctor. Scars not seen. You read it until the candle dies.

events.text: {npc}, an herb-seller who walks the same circuit of villages every month, comes to you white-faced. "Willow Ford is empty," {he} says. "Two hundred people. I was there the morning after. The rice was still warm in the pots, and the dogs were gone too." Nobody else will go back. {npc} will not go alone.

mem.note: was not left to go alone

effects.log: You set out that afternoon. {npc} walks very close to you the whole way.

choices.text: Ask what {he} has told the county

effects.log: "Everything," {npc} says. "The county said to forget it. That is why I came to you."

choices.text: Say it is the county's business

effects.log: {npc} walks away without a word.

events.text: Willow Ford is silent. Doors stand open, the hearths are cold, a child's wooden horse lies in the road. But {npc} notices it first: nothing has been stolen. The savings jars under the floors are gone, and the ancestor tablets from every house shrine. "Thieves take silver," {npc} says. "Only families take their dead."

effects.log: The headman's tablets are gone too, and a letter half-burned in the hearth: "...the morning of the tenth..."
You carry it with you. Someone will want it back.

events.text: Behind the village, the dry streambed climbs into the hills, and once you know how to look, the whole village is written on its stones: two hundred people walking carefully from rock to rock so as to leave no prints in the mud. Old people helped up the steep places. Small feet carried. {npc} kneels and touches a scuff on a boulder. "They were afraid," {he} says. "Not of a ghost. Of someone who would follow."

effects.log: Near the top you find a cold fire, carefully hidden, and a child's ribbon caught on a thorn.

choices.text: Turn back before you are seen

effects.log: If they are hiding, the last thing they need is a stranger leading anyone to them.

events.text: Your sect has eyes in more places than any county. A brother of the sect's scouts, two valleys over, saw a long line of villagers on the mountain road at dawn that morning, carrying bundles and old people, and lost them in the mist. {npc} lets out a breath {he} has held for a month. "Alive," {he} says. "They were alive."

choices.text: Ask the scouts to say nothing

effects.log: The sect agrees, as a favour to you. Whatever the villagers ran from, it will not hear it from you.

choices.text: Ask where the mist lies thickest

effects.log: A hidden valley, the scouts say, where the old charcoal-burners used to live.

events.text: The county ledgers are dull until one entry, in a fresh hand: "Willow Ford, the tenth: all able persons from fifteen to forty to be taken for the border works." The magistrate's press-gang was due the morning the village emptied. {npc} closes the ledger very carefully. "They did not vanish," {he} says. "They ran."

effects.log: You copy the magistrate's order word for word. It may be worth a great deal to the right people.
Magistrate Cho, newly come, ambitious, owed favours in the capital.

events.text: In a hidden valley of the old charcoal-burners you find them: two hundred people in huts of branches, thin and frightened and alive. They came here the night before the press-gang. When they see {npc}, the children run to {him} for the sweets {he} always carries. The headman asks you, very quietly, if you have come to take them back.

choices.text: Bring them home under your protection

effects.log: You walk them home in daylight and stand in the road when Magistrate Cho's men come. The men go away. Willow Ford lights its hearths.

choices.text: Take the order to the prefect

effects.log: You lay the copied order before the prefect, and Magistrate Cho is recalled. The villagers come home a month later.

events.text: The headman listens, then looks at you hard. "You are the kind of person magistrates fear," the old headman says. "Good. Then we will come home behind you." You do not say what you are, or what you have done in other places. Today you are the person standing between two hundred people and the border works.

effects.log: You visit the magistrate at night. The order is torn up by morning, and Magistrate Cho asks for a post far away.
You walk at the front of the line. Nobody stops you. Nobody dares.

events.text: Your answer reaches the villages around Willow Ford, and it frightens them: an array, a plague, the county covering it up. Families pack their carts. {npc} comes to you, furious. "Now everyone is running," {he} says, "and none of them knows from what."

choices.text: Go village to village and calm them

effects.log: It takes a month of talking. Most carts are unpacked by the end of it.
Somewhere in the county's books is the real reason. You go back to them.

events.text: {npc} comes to you in mourning white with a plain grey sword wrapped in a quilt. "My spouse bought it," {he} says. "Seven owners. Seven dead. Everyone says it is cursed, and the pawnshop wants it back, and I will not give it to them until someone tells me what killed the person I married."

choices.text: Take the sword and look at it

effects.log: It is a good plain sword, well balanced, with no name and no stain. It feels like a sword, nothing more.
{npc} bows very low. You are, {he} says, the first person who has not told {him} to burn it.
{npc} wraps the sword back up and leaves without a word.

events.text: When {npc} unwraps the grey sword, you know before you touch it that it is only a sword. Your soul has met this kind of curse before, in another life, and the curse had hands. You do not remember the face. You remember the lesson: when a thing kills over and over, look for who profits.

effects.log: "The pawnshop on Lantern Street," {npc} says. "It always goes back to the pawnshop."

choices.text: Keep the thought to yourself for now

effects.log: You say only that you will look into it. {npc} sees something hard come into your face.

events.text: The county's death records are kind to you: seven owners in nine years, a merchant, a guard captain, a wandering swordsman, two brothers, a teacher, and {npc}'s spouse. All died alone at night in their own rooms, the sword unsheathed beside them. Not one had a wound from it. {npc} reads the list and sits down on the floor.

choices.text: Look at who found the bodies

effects.log: Neighbours, servants, a landlord. Nobody connected to anybody.

choices.text: Look at what happened to the sword after

effects.log: Every time, within a month, the sword went back to the same pawnshop on Lantern Street.

events.text: You sleep with the grey sword beside you for a week in a room at the inn, the shutters loose. On the sixth night, in the third watch, a shadow comes to the window, sees you sitting awake with the blade across your knees, and goes away again without a sound. {npc}, asleep in the next room, hears nothing.

effects.log: Gone over the roofs. But a scrap of cloth hangs on the shutter nail: a pawnbroker's grey.

choices.text: Stay still and remember the shape

effects.log: Short, light-footed, old. Someone who has done this before.

events.text: The shadow comes to your window on the sixth night, sees what is sitting there in the dark, and stops dead. You let it see your eyes. Your realm is not something a back-alley killer meets twice. It is gone before you can rise, and in the morning the pawnshop on Lantern Street does not open its shutters.

effects.log: {npc} listens with both hands pressed over {his} mouth. "Not a curse," {he} says. "A person."
You find a roof across the street from it and wait.

events.text: From a roof across Lantern Street you watch the pawnshop for a month. Old Man Ok the pawnbroker sells the grey sword to a young guard who cannot believe the price. That night, the old man's shop is dark and the old man is not at home. You are on the guard's roof before the old man is.

effects.log: The young guard opens the door with a candle. Down the street, a short figure turns and walks quickly away.
You see enough to be sure. The old man sees nothing at all.

events.text: In front of the magistrate, with {npc} standing in mourning white at your side, you lay it out: Old Man Ok the pawnbroker sold the same plain sword eight times, and seven times went in the night to the buyer's window with a needle of sleeping poison, and took the sword back, and sold it again. A curse made it easy. Nobody looks for a murderer when they can blame a sword.

mem.note: got the truth about the death in the family

effects.log: {npc} takes it and does not weep. "It is only a sword," {he} says. "It was only ever a sword."

choices.text: Break the sword over your knee

effects.log: The crowd gasps when it snaps. The legend dies with the blade, and Old Man Ok goes to the magistrate's cells.

events.text: "Cursed," you said, or "a ghost", and the town believes you. The grey sword is thrown into the river, and the pawnbroker on Lantern Street nods sadly in the crowd. {npc} looks at the water a long time. "Then nobody killed my spouse," {he} says. "Only a sword." {He} does not sound as if {he} believes it.

effects.log: It takes two days and some silver. The sword comes up clean, and you start again.

choices.text: Watch who smiles in the crowd

effects.log: One face in the crowd looks pleased. You remember it.

events.text: {npc} has poled the ferry at the Nine Willows crossing for as long as anyone remembers, and the old ones say for longer than that. Today, halfway across, {npc} stops poling and looks at you, and the river runs on under the boat. "Have we met?" {he} asks. You have not. {He} keeps looking anyway.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how long {he} has kept the ferry

effects.log: "A long time," {npc} says, and smiles, and does not say how long.

choices.text: Look at {his} hands on the pole

effects.log: Young hands. Old calluses. Calluses take a lifetime.

choices.text: Look away and let the crossing end

effects.log: The boat bumps the far bank. {npc} watches you go up the steps.

events.text: In the county hall hangs a painting of the Nine Willows crossing, two hundred years old by the seal in its corner. The willows are smaller. The landing is wood, not stone. And the ferryman in the painting, poling a boat full of pilgrims, has the face of {npc}, exactly, down to the scar on {his} chin.

choices.text: Ask the clerk about the painter

effects.log: The painter died two hundred years ago. The clerk says the ferryman is "a family likeness".

choices.text: Stand in front of it a long time

effects.log: In the painting, the ferryman is looking at the far bank, as if waiting for someone.

events.text: You ride the ferry at night, alone, and ask {npc} straight out. For a long while there is only the pole and the water. Then: "I am waiting to carry someone across," {npc} says, "who once carried me." {He} looks at you the way {he} did the first day, as if you were a word {he} has almost remembered.

effects.log: "I never knew the name," {npc} says. "I knew the back, and the cold, and the voice telling me not to let go."
You take the second pole. You row well together, as if you had done it before.

events.text: The temple at the crossing keeps a record of the great flood two hundred years ago: the river over the willows, the village gone, and a stranger who swam the flood with a drowning boy on their back, put the boy on the bank, and died that night of the cold. No name. The boy lived. The last piece is not in this life: the one the ferryman waits for has to come back to the river first.

choices.text: Leave the record where it is

effects.log: You do not tell {npc} yet. Not until you know who the stranger was.
The temple keeper lights it for you. Somewhere in your chest, something old and cold lets go.

events.text: The ferry at the Nine Willows crossing is halfway over when {npc} lets the pole trail in the water and begins to weep without a sound. You have never seen this river in this life. {npc} has. "It is you," {he} says. "The back is different, and the face, and the voice. It is you."

effects.log: You pole the ferry the rest of the way. {npc} sits in the bottom of the boat and laughs and weeps at once.
The flood, the cold, the back, the voice. You listen, and your soul listens harder.

events.text: You say it on the landing at dawn: {npc} was the drowning boy, and waited two hundred years at this crossing to carry across the soul that once carried {him}, and that soul is yours. {npc} sets down the pole. For the first time in two hundred years, the ferryman looks tired. "Now I can be old," {he} says.

choices.text: Let {npc} carry you across one last time

effects.log: The last crossing is slow and quiet. On the far bank {npc} ties up the boat and walks away up the road, already greyer.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to come with you instead

effects.log: "Where you go, then," {npc} says, "for as long as I have left." It is not long. It is enough.

events.text: "A pact," you say, or "a ghost", and {npc} looks at you with something that is almost pity. "No," {he} says. "You of all people should know better." The crossing is very cold that evening, and {npc} does not speak again until the far bank.

effects.log: "There is nothing to forgive," {npc} says. "Only something to remember."
You come back every day for a month. {npc} lets you.

events.text: A month of asking, and the trail ends in a burned house and a neighbour who moved away years ago. {npc} sits on the step beside you. "Dead end," {he} says. "We wait, then. Trails warm again, if you are patient."

effects.log: You write down everything you have so far, so that none of it is lost in the waiting.

choices.text: Walk the dead end once more

effects.log: Nothing new. But you know the street well now, and that may matter later.

events.text: Word gets round that you are chasing a ghost story, and the teahouses enjoy it. Someone has written a comic song. {npc} hears it in the market and goes red to the ears on your behalf.

effects.log: You laugh louder than anyone. The song loses its sting.
Let them sing. The truth does not care who is laughing.

events.text: The lead goes bad all at once: a loose stair, a guard dog, a fall in the dark. You come away bruised, and {npc} binds your arm with a strip of {his} own sleeve and scolds you the whole time.

effects.log: You let {him}. It is a kind of care.
You are not fine. {npc} knows it, and says nothing.

events.text: Nothing again. {npc} has started to look at you the way people look at a lamp that keeps going out. "Perhaps we are asking the wrong questions," {he} says, carefully, and you hear what {he} does not say.

effects.log: {npc} tells you, at length. Some of it is good. You say so.

choices.text: Insist you are on the right track

effects.log: {npc} nods and says nothing more about it.

events.text: The friend, the sect or the official door you leaned on gave nothing, and it cost them to try. {npc} hears about it and winces. "Every door you knock on remembers the knock," {he} says.

choices.text: Send a gift to make it right

effects.log: A small gift, an apology. It does not undo the cost, but it is noticed.
Some doors close. Others open. You go on.

events.text: The second wrong answer is the last. {npc} does not argue with you this time. {He} only gathers up the notes and the copied pages and the drawings, ties them with string, and puts them in your hands. "Keep these," {he} says. "Someone will finish it someday. Maybe even you."

effects.log: You keep it all. Perhaps a later life will open it.

mem.note: keeps the case for someone else

effects.log: {npc} takes it, and promises to keep it for whoever comes next.
